summary: Citizens of around 100 visa-exempt countries — including the EU, US, UK, Canada and Australia — can visit Israel for up to 90 days but must obtain an ETA-IL electronic travel authorization before boarding; other nationalities need a B/2 visitor visa from an Israeli consulate, and nationals of several states with no relations with Israel are effectively barred.

defaultStayWindow.text: The Population and Immigration Authority states that an approved ETA-IL lets you “stay for up to 90 days per visit” — the allowance is per entry, not a running total, so leaving and returning starts it again. The authority does not say whether the days of arrival and departure are counted, so we count both.

source.name: Israel Population and Immigration Authority — ETA-IL

fee.notes: Per traveler, paid online; the fee has at times been waived during the rollout. The current amount is shown on the official site.

source.name: Israel Population and Immigration Authority — About ETA-IL

fee.notes: The Foreign Ministry's 2026 consular tariff for a B/2 visitor visa at Israeli missions: USD 32 or €28, charged in local currency. Indian and Sri Lankan passport holders living in India or Sri Lanka can instead apply online through the eVisa-B2 pilot, for a 105 NIS handling fee.

source.name: Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs — Fees for consular services (B/2 Visitor Visa, 2026)

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 3 months from the date you arrive in Israel.

source.name: Israel Population and Immigration Authority — About ETA-IL

travelInsurance.text: No official page states an insurance requirement for visa-exempt visitors travelling on an ETA-IL. Applicants for an eVisa-B2 tourist visa must show health insurance valid in Israel for the whole visit. Medical care is expensive either way, so check that any policy covers the current security situation.

source.name: Population and Immigration Authority — eVisa-B2 tourist visa: required documents

onwardTicket.text: Applicants for an eVisa-B2 tourist visa must upload a round-trip ticket to Israel. No official page states a ticket requirement for visa-exempt visitors travelling on an ETA-IL.

source.name: Population and Immigration Authority — eVisa-B2 tourist visa: required documents

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published. eVisa-B2 applicants must prove sufficient funds for the visit with bank statements for the last three months, a bank letter, or another document showing the funds. Border officers may ask any visitor about means and accommodation.

source.name: Population and Immigration Authority — eVisa-B2 tourist visa: required documents

currencyLimits.text: Cash and other means of payment (bank and travellers' cheques, bearer securities, negotiable instruments, payment cards) worth ILS 50,000 or more must be declared on entry and exit at any border crossing, and ILS 12,000 or more at the Nizana, Jordan River, Yitzhak Rabin, Taba and Allenby land crossings. At Allenby the declaration is made through a separate online service.

source.name: Israel Tax Authority (gov.il) — Declare bringing money into and out of Israel (Customs form 84)
source.instrument: Prohibition on Money Laundering Law, s. 9

payments.text: No official source we could read describes card acceptance in Israel. Australia's Smartraveller says ATMs are widely available; the Government of Canada notes they may not accept Canadian cards.

safety.text: Israel is a modern, orderly country, but the security situation can change quickly: government advisories warn particularly about areas near Gaza and the Lebanese border, and rocket alerts can occur elsewhere. Learn how Home Front Command alerts work, follow local instructions, and check your government's advisory before and during your trip.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Israel travel advice

tips.text: The UK FCDO says visitors arriving at Ben Gurion Airport get an entry card instead of a passport stamp; at other entry points you may get a card or a stamp. Keep the card with your passport until you leave — it is evidence that you entered legally, and you may need it if you cross into Palestine.

The UK FCDO lists three land crossings with Jordan — Allenby/King Hussein Bridge, the northern Jordan River/Sheikh Hussein crossing and the southern Yitzhak Rabin/Wadi Araba crossing — and says they may be restricted or closed at short notice. Check the Israel Airports Authority's updates before you go.
The UK FCDO says you may face lengthy personal questioning and baggage searches at security when you enter and leave Israel. Allow plenty of time at the airport.

Shabbat runs from sunset on Friday to Saturday evening. Australia's Smartraveller says driving is restricted in Orthodox neighbourhoods and public access to them is usually restricted, and the UK FCDO advises against driving into ultra-Orthodox areas of Jerusalem on Shabbat. Plan travel around it.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Israel?
faq.answer: If you are from one of the roughly 100 visa-exempt countries — the EU, US, UK, Canada, Australia, most of Latin America and others — you do not need a visa for stays of up to 90 days, but you must obtain an ETA-IL electronic travel authorization online before boarding. Most other nationalities need a B/2 visitor visa from an Israeli embassy or consulate; citizens of Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Libya, Syria and Yemen are not admitted except with rare individual permission, and ordinary tourism is effectively closed to Afghan, Pakistani, Saudi, Somali and Sudanese passport holders.

faq.question: What is ETA-IL and how do I get one?
faq.answer: ETA-IL is Israel's electronic travel authorization, mandatory for visa-exempt visitors. Apply at israel-entry.piba.gov.il with your passport details; the fee is ILS 25 per traveler and the authority says a reply usually arrives within 24 to 72 hours, sometimes within minutes. It is valid for two years (or until your passport expires) and covers multiple visits of up to 90 days.

faq.question: Does Israel stamp your passport?
faq.answer: Not at Ben Gurion Airport: the UK FCDO says visitors arriving there get an entry card instead of a passport stamp, while at other entry points you may get either a card or a stamp. Exit and entry stamps from neighbouring countries' land borders can still show the visit.

faq.question: Will visiting Israel prevent me from entering other countries?
faq.answer: It can. The UK FCDO says an Israeli stamp or other evidence of travel to Israel may get you refused entry to Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Kuwait — for Iran this includes stamps from other countries' border crossings with Israel. Entry to Israel through Ben Gurion normally leaves no stamp, but check before planning onward travel to such countries.

faq.question: Is it safe to visit Israel right now?
faq.answer: Conditions vary with the regional situation. Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and the main tourist areas function normally most of the time, but government advisories warn against areas near Gaza and the northern border, and rocket alerts can occur with little notice. Check your government's current advice, buy insurance that covers the situation, and follow Home Front Command instructions while in the country.
